spans.content: Competitive ability, body size and geographical
range size in small mammals
Douglas S. Glazier1* and Sara E. Eckert2 1Department of Biology, Juniata College,
Huntingdon, PA, USA, 2 United States Department of Interior, United States Geological
Survey, Las Vegas Field Station, South Paradise Road, Las Vegas, NV, USA
Abstract
Aim Why are some species widespread and abundant while others are restricted and
rare? Darwin (1859) and others have claimed that some species have become widespread
because they are competitively dominant over related, geographically restricted species.
An alternative hypothesis is that wide-ranging species are ecological generalists that have
been able to opportunistically colonize many kinds of new, disturbed and/or marginal
habitats, whereas related narrow-ranging species are ecological specialists that compet-
itively dominate speci®c kinds of relatively stable habitats/resources. We tested these
opposing hypotheses using small mammals, for which considerable data on competitive
interactions and geographical range sizes are available.
Location North America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia.
Methods We analysed data for forty-three competitive interactions between congeneric
species in twenty genera, seven families, and four orders of small mammals. Competitive
dominance was identi®ed from both ®eld and laboratory experiments, which were
lumped because they showed similar results.
Results We found that (1) when all studies were analysed as individual data points,
species with smaller geographical ranges tended to be dominant over congeneric species
with larger geographical ranges, (2) lumping of interaction pairs sharing one or more of
the same species yielded a similar result, (3) lumping all interactions involving the same
genus also showed the same result, although it was not statistically signi®cant, probably
because of the small sample size resulting from this attempt to remove phylogenetic
effects. Examination of the taxonomic relationships of the studied genera revealed no
obvious phylogenetic effects on the relationship of competitive dominance with
geographical range size. Furthermore, although body-size differences appeared to have
played a role in the results observed, they cannot completely explain them.
Main conclusions We tentatively conclude that Darwin's hypothesis is falsi®ed for
small mammals, while the alternative hypothesis that geographically restricted species
are competitively dominant over related widespread species receives some support.
Keywords
behavioural dominance, competition, congeneric species, geographical range size,
mammals, meta-analysis.

INTRODUCTION
Nearly 150 years ago, Darwin (1859) lamented in his book
On the Origin of Species: `Who can explain why one species
ranges widely and is very numerous, and why another
species has a narrow range and is rare? Yet these relations
are of the highest importance, for they determine the present
welfare, and, as I believe, the future success and modi®cation
of every inhabitant of this world' (p. 6). Despite this
inspirational call for further research in one of the most
famous scienti®c books of all time, we are still a long way
from answering Darwin's fundamental question.
One approach to this problem, which has received
increasing attention during the last two decades, is to search
for biological correlates of geographical range size (see
reviews of Kunin & Gaston, 1993; Gaston, 1994; Kunin &
Gaston, 1997). Some factors that have been identi®ed as
being at least potentially important within speci®c taxa
include dispersal/colonization ability (e.g. Glazier, 1980;
Reaka, 1980; Oakwood et al., 1993; Kelly & Woodward,
1996; GutieÂrrez & MeneÂndez, 1997; Dennis et al., 2000),
niche breadth (e.g. Glazier, 1980; Brown, 1984, 1995;
NovotnyÂ, 1991; Pagel et al., 1991; Kitahara & Fujii, 1994;
Hecnar, 1999; Pyron, 1999; Dennis et al., 2000; KruÈ ger &
McGavin, 2000), trophic level/feeding habits (e.g. Brown,
1981; Rapoport, 1982; Pagel et al., 1991; Arita et al., 1997),
body size (e.g. Glazier, 1980; Reaka, 1980; Brown, 1981,
1995; Aizen & Patterson, 1990; Arita et al., 1997; GutieÂrrez
& MeneÂndez, 1997; Hecnar, 1999; Pyron, 1999; KruÈ ger &
McGavin, 2000), life form (e.g. Oakwood et al., 1993; Kelly
& Woodward, 1996), genetic variation (e.g. Karron, 1997),
and life-history traits (e.g. Glazier, 1980, 1986; Aizen &
Patterson, 1990; Oakwood et al., 1993; Dennis et al., 2000).
However, we are unaware of any comparative studies
designed to test whether geographical range size is related to
competitive ability. This is surprising because two prominent
contrasting views on the competitive ability of widely vs.
narrowly distributed species are present in the ecological and
biogeographical literature. On one hand, Darwin (1859),
and many others after him (e.g. Brown, 1957; Darlington,
have argued that widespread species and higher taxa have
superior `®tness', and thus have attained their large ranges
by out-competing restricted, `less ®t' taxa for geographical
territory. The common ®nding that widespread species are
usually more abundant than related restricted species in local
habitats has been offered in support of this view (Brown,
On the other hand, some biologists have suggested that
broadly distributed species may be competitively inferior to
related, more narrowly distributed species. According to this
view, the greater ecological specialization of restricted
species has given them enhanced competitive ability. Wide-
ranging species are thought to be opportunistic colonists of
new, disturbed and/or marginal habitats scattered over wide
areas, and as such are replaced by more ecologically
specialized, restricted species in relatively stable habitats
(e.g. Wilson, 1961; Ricklefs & Cox, 1972, 1978; Glazier,
1980, 1986, 1987; NovotnyÂ, 1991; Thomas, 1991; Dennis
et al., 2000; references therein). This view is supported by
two well-known models: the r- vs. K-selection model
(MacArthur & Wilson, 1967) and the included niche model
(Miller, 1967; Morse, 1974, 1980; Henttonen & Hansson,
1984). According to the r- vs. K-selection model, species that
use relatively unstable habitats or resources are selected for
high colonizing ability and rapid population growth,
whereas species that use relatively stable habitats or
resources are selected for high competitive ability and
ef®cient use of resources. The included niche model predicts
that ecologically specialized species should out-compete
coexisting generalized species, which are consequently
forced to occupy marginal niche space. Both of these models
can explain why geographically restricted species may be
competitively dominant over related widespread species.
Of course, a third possibility is that geographical range
size is unrelated to competitive ability. This may be because
other biological, historical, or environmental factors are
more important, or because relative competitive ability is so
habitat- or taxon-speci®c that no consistent regional differ-
ences between wide- vs. narrow-ranging species can be
discerned.
These alternative hypotheses were tested by comparing the
relative competitive abilities of congeneric species of small
mammals with different geographical range sizes. Small
mammals were chosen for this study because their geo-
graphical range sizes are well known, and considerable data
on interspeci®c competitive interactions are available. Only
pairs of congeneric species were studied to maximize the
likelihood of observing competitive effects and to minimize
extraneous phylogenetic effects.
METHODS
We analysed data for forty-three competitive interactions
between congeneric species in twenty genera, seven families
and four orders of small mammals (Appendix 1). Three kinds
of studies were included and initially analysed separately:
laboratory studies, ®eld studies, and studies that combined
laboratory and ®eld experiments.
Different investigators had different speci®c de®nitions of
competitive dominance, but in all studies a dominant species
was regarded as having a greater adverse effect on a
subordinate species, than the reverse. The laboratory studies
typically examined the relative frequency of agonistic and
submissive behaviours in staged dyadic encounters, the more
aggressive species being considered dominant (e.g. Sheppard,
1971; Blaustein & Risser, 1976; Montgomery, 1978;
Dempster & Perrin, 1990; Livoreil et al., 1993). This
approach was a reliable way to measure aggressiveness (i.e.
interference competition), because it is robust to variation in
testing protocols (Harper & Batzli, 1997). Most of the ®eld
studies either made direct observations of relative beha-
vioural dominance in natural areas (e.g. Chappell, 1978)
baited areas (e.g. Congdon, 1974), or outdoor pens or cages
(e.g. Hoffmeyer, 1973; Wolff et al., 1983; Fitzgerald &
Keith, 1990), or inferred competitive dominance from

studies involved spatial or temporal comparisons of relative

unmanipulated plots (e.g. Tast, 1968; Hallett, 1982; Viitala,
1984; Norrdahl & KorpimaÈki, 1993) or plots or enclosures
where competing species had been introduced (e.g. Vaughan
& Hansen, 1964; Ziv et al., 1993), removed (e.g. Chappell,
1978; Holbrook, 1979; Gliwicz, 1981), or both (Dickman,
1986). Two ®eld studies inferred competitive dominance
from regional analyses of apparent competitive exclusion
among species (Kennerly, 1959; Miller, 1964). Results were
lumped for multiple studies examining competitive interac-
tions between the same two species. If the results were
con¯icting they were resolved, as explained in Appendix 2.
Relative geographical range sizes (larger vs. smaller) were
determined using Hall (1981) and Nowak (1999). Four
interaction pairs (Rattus rattus L./R. norvegicus Berkenhout,
Tamias dorsalis Baird/T. umbrinus J.A. Allen, Clethriono-
mys gapperi Vigors/C. rutilus Pallas and Ctenomys talarum
Thomas/C. australis Rusconi) were excluded from the
analyses because the geographical range sizes of the species
in each pair were virtually the same (Barnett & Spencer,
1951; Brown, 1971; McPhee, 1984; Comparatore et al.,
1992; Vassallo, 1993). Four other interaction pairs (Micro-
tus pennsylvanicus Ord/M. ochrogaster Wagner, M. penn-
sylvanicus/M. montanus Peale, Peromyscus maniculatus
Wagner/P. truei Shufeldt and Sylvilagus ¯oridanus J.A.
Allen/S. transitionalis Bangs) were also omitted because no
dominance hierarchy could be demonstrated (Getz, 1962;
Koplin & Hoffman, 1968; Miller, 1969; Murie, 1971;
Grant, 1972; Stoecker, 1972; Krebs, 1977; Llewellyn, 1980;
Probert & Litvaitis, 1996).
Body size was examined because it can contribute to
competitive dominance (Miller, 1967; Grant, 1972; Morse,
1974; Viitala, 1977; Henttonen & Hansson, 1984; Persson,
1985). Relative body masses (larger vs. smaller) were
determined using data in Silva & Downing (1995).
G-tests of independence (using Williams's correction,
following Sokal & Rohlf, 1995) were used to test for
relationships between competitive dominance and geograph-
ical range size, between competitive dominance and body
mass, and between geographical range size and body mass.
The tests were made in three ways. First, each interaction
pair was treated as a separate data point. Secondly,
interaction pairs involving the same species were lumped
and counted as a single data point. Thirdly, interaction pairs
involving the same genus were lumped and counted as a
single data point. In this lumping process, when studies did
not agree the prevailing trend was used. If there was no
prevailing trend, the data were omitted. This rarely occurred:
once when examining competitive dominance in relation to
geographical range size, once when examining competitive
dominance in relation to body mass, and thrice when
examining geographical range size in relation to body mass.
The last two methods were employed to minimize
phylogenetic bias (Harvey & Pagel, 1991). An exploration
of possible phylogenetic effects was also made by comparing
results in different taxa using the taxonomic scheme of
Nowak (1999).
RESULTS
The forty-three interaction pairs used in this study, and their
taxonomic af®nities, are summarized in Appendix 1. Results
of ®eld and laboratory studies were similar: relatively
restricted species were more often competitively dominant
over congeneric widespread species than vice versa
(Table 1). These results were signi®cant for ®eld studies
and for all studies combined, and marginally signi®cant for
laboratory studies. As the ®eld and laboratory studies
revealed similar results they were analysed together in the
rest of this section. The results were also not affected by the
fact that in some interaction pairs the species with a smaller
distribution was still quite wide-ranging (e.g. Sorex araneus
L., Lepus europaeus Pallas and P. leucopus Ra®nesque).
Competitive dominance and geographical range size were
signi®cantly inversely associated for all interaction pairs,
including when interaction pairs sharing the same species
were lumped (Table 2). A similar result was observed when
all interaction pairs in the same genus were lumped,
although it was not signi®cant, probably because of the
small sample size resulting from this lumping process
(Table 2). Examination of the taxonomic relationships of
the studied genera revealed no obvious phylogenetic effects
on the relationship of competitive dominance with geo-
graphical range size, although this conclusion should be
re-examined when more data on non-rodent competitive

Nevertheless, for both rodent and non-rodent interactions,

DISCUSSION
This study tested whether geographical range size is related
to the relative competitive ability of congeneric species of
small mammals. There are three possibilities: (1) widespread
species are competitively dominant over relatively restricted
species, (2) restricted species are dominant over relatively
widespread species, or (3) there is no association between
geographical range size and competitive ability. The present
analysis suggests that the second alternative is the most
important one. Using three methods of data analysis,
competitive dominance was found to be more prevalent
among geographically restricted species than among related
widespread species (Tables 1 and 2).
According to Glazier (1987), restricted species have
tended to evolve in relatively stable habitats where
K-selection for high competitive ability is favoured. This
hypothesis is supported by the ®nding that restricted species
of rodents and moths tend to have more stable populations
than related widespread species (Glazier, 1986). It is further
supported by an extensive comparative analysis of the life-
history traits and habitat distribution of Peromyscus species
(Glazier, 1980). Widely distributed species in this genus tend
to occur more frequently in new, disturbed and/or marginal
habitats than narrowly distributed species. Moreover,
the habitat distribution of the widespread species tends to

shrink at localities with coexisting restricted species, as
would be expected if the restricted species were competit-
ively dominant. In addition, the restricted species have
signi®cantly lower reproductive potentials, as predicted from
K-selection operating in relatively stable populations.
What gives many restricted small mammal species a
competitive advantage over their more wide-ranging rela-
tives? Ecological specialization, a common trait of narrowly
distributed species (e.g. Glazier, 1980), is probably involved.
Greater ecological specialization may permit a more ef®cient
use of resources (i.e. greater exploitative competition), or
may favour the evolution of greater aggressiveness (i.e.
interference competition) as a way of protecting specialized
niches from invasion by generalized species (Miller, 1967;
Colwell & Fuentes, 1975). Many studies have shown that
specialized species tend to have higher competitive ability
than related generalized species (e.g. Miller, 1967; Morse,
1974; Holbrook, 1978; Hallett, 1982). Further research is
needed to identify the precise mechanisms involved and their
relative importance.
The results of this study are consistent with two additional
general observations. First, most taxa include far more
restricted species than widespread species (e.g. Rapoport,
1982; Gaston, 1994; Brown, 1995). If widespread species
were competitively superior, they should have over-run the
habitats of most restricted species, causing their extinction.
That they have not attests to the ability of restricted species
to hold their own against widespread species (either through
superior competitive ability in speci®c habitats, or by
occupation of refugia protected by barriers).
Secondly, in most taxa, species with small ranges are
usually more numerous in the tropics than at higher latitudes
(e.g. Rapoport, 1982; Glazier, 1987; Stevens, 1989; Brown,
1995; Dynesius & Jansson, 2000; Gaston & Blackburn,
2000). If one assumes that interspeci®c competition is
generally more severe in the species-rich tropics, then the
survival there of legions of narrow-ranging species argues
against the idea that they are inferior competitors.
The included niche model of Miller (1967) is consistent
with the present results, as well. Miller (1967) and Morse
(1974, 1980) have reviewed many avian and mammalian
examples of specialized species having smaller niche spaces
enclosed within the larger niche spaces of more generalized
related species. In most of these cases, it is the specialized
species that are competitively dominant. They also note that
many of these specialized species have larger body sizes.
Larger animals are almost always better at interference
competition than smaller animals (Persson, 1985). This is
also true for the small mammals included in this study. Large
species are more often competitively dominant over related
smaller species than vice versa (Table 3).
One may argue that the association between competitive
dominance and geographical range size observed in this
study is merely a secondary result of both being correlated
with body size. However, although competitive dominance
is signi®cantly related to body size, geographical range size is
only weakly related to body size (Table 4). Thus, although
body-size differences appear to have contributed to the
association between competitive dominance and geograph-
ical range size, they do not completely explain this pattern.
Larger body size may very well be one of the several traits
that restricted species have evolved to make themselves more
effective competitors with relatively generalized, widespread
species that are constantly threatening to invade their niche
spaces.
The present results contradict the view of Darwin (1859),
Brown (1984) and others that widespread generalized
species are competitively dominant over restricted special-
ized species. Although Brown presented no data on relative
competitive ability, he inferred that widespread species are
competitively dominant over restricted species because
usually they are more abundant in local habitats. According
to Brown (1984, 1995), a trade-off between being special-
ized vs. generalized (jack of all trades, but master of none)
may not exist because, if it operated, specialized restricted
species should be more abundant locally than generalized
widespread species, which is generally not true.
However, a positive association between local abundance
and geographical range does not necessarily mean that
widespread species are competitively dominant over related
restricted species. Plausible counter-arguments can be made
for both exploitative and interference competition. For
example, specialized restricted species could be more ef®cient
resource exploiters than generalized widespread species, and
still have smaller local populations because they use rarer or
lower quality resources. In addition, species selection among
restricted, locally rare species may have put a high premium
on effective interference competition because it ensures that
the limited resources on which these species have specialized
will not be usurped by relatively generalized species.
Restricted species are on the edge of extinction, and thus
those that have evolved behavioural dominance are more
likely to have survived than those that did not.
Thus, unlike Brown (1984, 1995), we suggest that trade-
offs between being specialized vs. generalized have been
important in determining the different geographical range
sizes of related species. Other trade-offs, such as those
between competitive ability (enhanced in restricted species)
and dispersal/colonization pro®ciency (enhanced in wide-
spread species), may also be important. Such trade-offs have
been assumed in many species-coexistence models (e.g.
Levins & Culver, 1971; Horn & MacArthur, 1972;
Hastings, 1980; Tilman et al., 1997; Holmes & Wilson,
1998; Kinzig et al., 1999), and have been invoked to explain
several ecological and biogeographical patterns, including
succession (Tilman, 1990, 1994), species packing in com-
munities (Kinzig et al., 1999), the taxon cycle (Wilson,
1961; Ricklefs & Cox, 1972; Glazier, 1980), effects of
habitat destruction on species loss (Tilman, 1994; Tilman
et al., 1997), and the tendency of many widespread species
to inhabit new, disturbed and/or marginal, species-poor
habitats in contrast to related restricted species that prefer-
entially occupy relatively stable, species-rich habitats (e.g.
Glazier, 1980, 1986; NovotnyÂ, 1991; references therein).
Considerable empirical evidence for colonization-competi-
tion trade-offs exists, as well (see Holmes & Wilson, 1998).

The generalist vs. specialist and colonization vs. compe-
tition trade-offs may act in concert with other trade-offs
resulting from r- vs. K-selection to in¯uence patterns of
geographical range sizes among related species (see Glazier,
1980, 1986). In support, Bowers & Harris (1994) have
developed a metapopulation model showing that changing
environments favour generalists with good dispersal ability,
whereas constant environments favour specialists with high
ef®ciency of resource utilization. The model of Pulliam
(2000) also shows how dispersal ability and niche breadth
may be linked to determine species-distribution patterns.
Kitahara & Fujii (1994) have further argued that a synthesis
of the generalist vs. specialist and r- vs. K-selection dichot-
omies are needed to better understand the biodiversity and
structure of natural communities. Thus, the above trade-offs
may represent interrelated aspects of a syndrome of factors
that cause some species to be more widespread than other
species. Further exploration of how these trade-offs interact
to affect the geographical spread of a species may take us a
long way toward answering Darwin's fundamental question
quoted at the beginning of this paper. However, if the
present results are generally applicable, the answer may be
quite different from what Darwin anticipated.

Appendix 2 Explanations of decisions made when studies disagreed
Peromyscus leucopus vs. P. maniculatus.
Laboratory experiments and ®eld observations of Fitch (1963), Kantak (1983, 1996) and Long (1996) suggest that P. leucopus is dominant over
P. maniculatus. These studies were given priority because other studies have found no advantage of one species over the other (e.g. Brown,
1964; Wolff et al., 1983).
Sorex araneus vs. S. minutus.
The study of Dickman (1991) was given priority because he gave experimental evidence for currently acting competition, whereas Ellenbroek
(1980) claimed that competition between these species had only occurred in the past.
Tamias amoenus vs. T. speciosus.
The ®eld experiment of Chappell (1978) was given priority over the laboratory experiment of Heller (1971).
Thomomys bottae vs. T. talpoides.
The ®eld data of Miller (1964) and Vaughan & Hansen (1964) were given greater weight than the laboratory data of Baker (1974).
